questions.title: What is the difference between the "right-to-control theory" rejected in Ciminelli and the "fraudulent-inducement theory" upheld in Kousisis?
questions.question_body: I'm reading United States v. Constantinescu and the court spends a lot of time distinguishing between the "right-to-control theory" from Ciminelli v. United States and the "fraudulent-inducement theory" from Kousisis v. United States. The court says Ciminelli rejected the right-to-control theory because depriving someone of "valuable economic information" isn't a traditional property interest, but Kousisis upheld the fraudulent-inducement theory because it involves tricking victims into handing over money or property. I'm struggling to understand the practical difference between these two theories. In both cases, the defendant is lying to the victim to get something of value, right? Why does it matter whether we characterize the victim's loss as "valuable economic information" versus "money or property"? Can someone explain the doctrinal distinction and why the Supreme Court treated them differently?

questions.title: Does securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1348 require the victim to suffer a net economic loss?
questions.question_body: In Constantinescu, the defendants argue that the indictment fails to allege intent to defraud because they intended to profit, not to harm their followers. The court rejects this argument, citing Kousisis for the proposition that fraud statutes don't require the victim to suffer net pecuniary loss. The court says the followers' receipt of "market-value securities" doesn't obviate the fraud charges. I'm confused about this concept. If the followers bought securities at an artificially inflated price due to the defendants' misrepresentations, didn't they suffer an economic loss? Or is the court saying that even if the securities were worth exactly what the followers paid, the fraud would still be complete? How does the "no net economic loss required" principle from Kousisis apply in this pump-and-dump context where the victims did seem to lose money?

questions.title: Why does the securities fraud statute (§ 1348) borrow concepts from mail and wire fraud statutes, and what does this mean for interpreting its elements?
questions.question_body: In Constantinescu, the Fifth Circuit notes that 18 U.S.C. § 1348 "borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes" and that courts often rely on mail and wire fraud cases when analyzing securities fraud charges. The court then cites United States v. Greenlaw for this proposition. I don't understand why this borrowing occurs. Is it because the statutes have similar text? Are there legislative history reasons? And practically, does this mean that any development in mail/wire fraud jurisprudence automatically applies to securities fraud under § 1348? Are there any limits to this borrowing principle, or could a future Supreme Court decision about mail fraud completely change how § 1348 is interpreted?

questions.title: What is the "mirror image" requirement in fraud cases, and why doesn't it apply here?
questions.question_body: The court in Constantinescu cites United States v. Baker for the proposition that fraud statutes do not impose a "mirror image" requirement where the victim's loss of money or property must equal the defendant's gain. I'm not sure I understand what this "mirror image" requirement is. Is the idea that in some fraud cases, the victim's loss and the defendant's gain are identical (like stealing $100 from someone's wallet), but in other cases they might not match? How does this relate to the Kousisis principle that a defendant can be liable even when providing something of equal value in return? And why is this concept relevant to the pump-and-dump scheme in Constantinescu where the defendants profited $114 million?

questions.title: What standard applies when reviewing the dismissal of an indictment, and why does the court take the indictment's allegations as true?
questions.question_body: In Constantinescu, the Fifth Circuit says it reviews the sufficiency of an indictment de novo and is "required to take the allegations of the indictment as true." The court then determines whether an offense has been stated. I'm confused about this procedural posture. If the district court dismissed the indictment, why does the appellate court take the allegations as true rather than evaluating whether the government actually has evidence to support them? Is this different from a motion for judgment of acquittal where the court would evaluate the evidence? Also, does this mean the defendants can still challenge the evidence at trial, or has the court essentially precluded them from arguing they didn't commit the alleged acts?

questions.title: What must an indictment allege to sufficiently charge securities fraud, and how does this case compare to cases where indictments were found deficient?
questions.question_body: The court in Constantinescu lists the requirements for a sufficient indictment: (1) enumerate each prima facie element, (2) fairly inform the defendant of the charges, and (3) provide a double jeopardy defense. The court then concludes the indictment sufficiently alleges a "scheme to defraud" and "intent to defraud." But I'm struggling to understand what makes this indictment sufficient when the district court found it deficient. The district court apparently concluded the indictment only alleged deprivation of "potentially valuable economic information" rather than a traditional property interest. What specific language in the indictment did the Fifth Circuit find sufficient to allege a scheme to deprive followers of money? Are there examples of indictments that failed to meet this standard, and what was missing from them?

questions.title: How does the "object of the fraud" requirement work, and what does it mean that defendants "had money in mind"?
questions.question_body: In Constantinescu, the court quotes Kousisis for the proposition that a defendant commits securities fraud when "obtaining the victim's money or property" was "an object of his fraud." Later, the court says the indictment's allegation that defendants pumped and dumped to gain a profit shows they "had money in mind." I'm confused about what "object" means here. Is this a subjective test (what the defendant actually intended) or an objective test (what a reasonable person would infer from the scheme)? Also, the phrase "had money in mind" seems informal—does this refer to a specific legal standard? If the defendants had multiple objectives (like gaining social media followers, building their brand, AND making money), does the fraud statute require money to be the primary object, or just one of several objects?
